study_identification.title: Using normative modeling to assess pharmacological treatment effect on brain state in patients with schizophrenia

study_characteristics.study_objective: To use normative models to assess the effect of pharmacological treatment on static and dynamic brain states in patients with schizophrenia, examining whether deviations from normative models are related to symptoms and whether baseline symptoms can predict deviation changes after treatment.

analysis_level.reason: The analysis was conducted at the network level using the Yeo-17 network template. Dynamic FC matrices were decomposed into 17 brain networks, and features were calculated for each network.
analysis_level.supporting_text: Then, each FC matrix was decomposed into 17 networks based on Yeo-17 network template (Yeo et al. 2011). The average FC connection strength (aFCS, mean of FC strength from all window-wise FC matrices) and fluctuation characteristic of connection strength (fFCS, average change of the window-wise FC strength) for each Yeo-17 network was yielded from time-varying dynamic FC matrices. Finally, each individual's dynamic FC pattern was represented by 34 features.

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: SPM12 (for Cam-CAN); SPM toolbox in MATLAB; Human Brainnetome Atlas parcellation; Yeo-17 network template
preprocessing_pipeline.reason: The preprocessing pipeline is clearly described. Cam-CAN data was preprocessed using Automatic Analysis calling SPM12. Patient data was processed using SPM toolbox in MATLAB with standard preprocessing steps. The Human Brainnetome Atlas was used for parcellation and Yeo-17 network template for network decomposition.
preprocessing_pipeline.supporting_text: The Cam-CAN provides us with the preprocessing neuroimaging data and the details are in the Supplementary Materials. The fMRI scans of the Cam-CAN dataset were preprocessed using Automatic Analysis calling functions from Statistical Parametric Mapping (SPM 12). For the imaging data of patients with schizophrenia and HCs, both structural and functional neuroimaging data were processed using spm toolbox in MATLAB (https://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm/). Spatial preprocessing involved reorienting to the imaginary line joining Anterior Commissure-Posterior Commissure, realignment, and slice-time correction. Brain tissue was segmented into gray matter/white matter/cerebrospinal fluid normalized to Montreal Neurological Institute space, and smoothed for spatial convolution with a 6-mm Gaussian kernel. For each individual, we computed dynamic FC matrices between all pairs of regions of the Human Brainnetome Atlas (Fan et al. 2016) using a sliding time window method (window length=60 s, step size = 1).

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study used 10-fold cross-validation on the Cam-CAN dataset. In this approach, 9 folds were used for training and 1 fold for validation, repeated 10 times. This is validation using non-independent data within the same domain (same dataset split into training and validation sets). The performance was assessed by examining the proportion of healthy individuals with supra/infra-deviation and normative certainty index.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Furthermore, to improve the generalizability of the model, we estimated the normative models of healthy individuals from Cam-CAN under 10-fold cross-validation. Specifically, the data were randomly divided into 10 folds. Nine-folds were utilized for building the model, whereas the remaining fold was employed to evaluate the general performance of the model. This process was repeated 10 times, with each fold being excluded once. The proportion of healthy individuals with supra-deviation (residing above 95% percentiles in normative models) was 2.75% for the aFCS features, and 2.91% for fFCS features. The average certainty for all participants from Cam-CAN was 0.991 for aFCS and 0.990 for fFCS.

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score with scaling coefficient based on the gap between 5th and 95th percentiles; normative certainty index; coefficient of variation
deviation_metric.reason: The deviation metric is clearly defined. A Z-score was calculated using a scaling coefficient defined by the gap between the 5th and 95th percentiles. Additional metrics include normative certainty index and coefficient of variation to assess heterogeneity.
deviation_metric.supporting_text: The gap between the 5th and 95th percentiles for a given age was as a scaling coefficient to normalize the feature deviation. For each individual, index i represented individual's ID, and j represented one of 34 features. Yij was the observed value for the i-th individual's j-th feature. Y50ij, Y95ij, and Y5ij were the predictive features in 50th, 95th, and 5th percentiles for the same age, respectively. Thus, the z-score in formula presents the deviation of a certain individual's a certain feature. We used a normative certainty index to quantify the performance of normative models. The normative certainty was measured by max(np/n, nn/n), where np and nn were the number of positive or negative Z-scores, and n is 10. Figure 2C shows the coefficients of variation (the ratio of the standard deviation to the absolute mean value) at network-level for bSCZ and aSCZ.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Pearson's correlations with permutation tests (n=5,000) were used to explore relationships between deviation profiles and clinical PANSS scores (5-factor model: positive, negative, disorganized, excited, depressed), controlling for sex, age, and head motion as covariates. General linear models were also employed. Patients were divided into two groups based on deviation changes after treatment (normalization vs. deviation groups), and group comparisons were conducted on baseline symptoms.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Patients showed greater deviations from normative models than healthy controls; those with milder positive and overall symptoms at baseline showed normalization of brain deviations after treatment, while others showed increased deviations; baseline depressive and overall symptom severity predicted static FC deviation changes, and baseline positive symptoms predicted dynamic FC deviation changes after treatment.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Patients with schizophrenia exceeded normative ranges more than healthy controls for brain network dynamic characteristics. Patients could be divided into two groups: a normalization group whose brain deviations decreased after 6-week treatment and showed milder positive (P=0.001, effect size=-1.21) and overall symptoms (P=0.03, effect size=-0.76) at baseline, and a deviation group whose brain deviations became more distinct after treatment. Pooling baseline and after-treatment data, deviations of sensorimotor network showed positive correlation with positive and overall symptoms; ventral attention network with overall symptoms; sub-DMNs with negative symptoms. Deviations of brain network dynamic fluctuations across all identified networks positively correlated with negative symptom severity. Baseline depressive symptoms negatively predicted static FC (aFCS) deviation changes, particularly in ventral/dorsal attention and somatomotor networks, suggesting patients with milder depressive symptoms were more likely to return to normal range. Baseline overall symptom severity also negatively correlated with fFCS deviations of sub-DMN. Baseline positive and overall symptoms negatively predicted dynamic fluctuation (fFCS) deviations of dorsal/ventral attention, salience, control, and DMN after treatment. Treatment decreased coefficients of variation for aFCS deviations (indicating convergence to mean state) but had less effect on dynamic fluctuation characteristics.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Small sample size (37 patients); unable to split healthy sample into independent training and validation sets, requiring use of 10-fold cross-validation which may introduce small bias; potential confounding effects from the 2-week drug washout period for some patients; heterogeneous medication regimens (mono- and dual-therapy with various antipsychotics).
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This is the first study to adopt normative modeling to assess brain changes affected by pharmacological treatment in schizophrenia. The study demonstrates the utility of normative modeling for understanding heterogeneity in treatment response at the individual level. The 5-factor PANSS model provided more nuanced symptom characterization. The finding that depressive symptoms predict static FC normalization while positive symptoms predict dynamic FC normalization suggests differential mechanisms of treatment effect on static vs. dynamic brain states.

general_notes.general_notes: The study used sliding window analysis for dynamic FC (window length=60s, step size=1). A total of 34 features were extracted per individual (17 networks × 2 features: aFCS and fFCS). Analysis included both baseline (bSCZ) and after-treatment (aSCZ) measurements, resulting in 68 features per patient across timepoints. Treatment duration was 6 weeks with various antipsychotic medications (8 drug-naïve first-episode patients, 7 with irregular medication willing to restart after 2-week washout, others with 2 weeks to 11 months medication discontinuation, mean±SD: 2.69±2.73 months). Medications included mono-therapy (n=27) and dual-therapy (n=8) with first- and second-generation antipsychotics; doses converted to chlorpromazine equivalents (mean 495.01±312.17 mg/d). Additional local healthy controls (n=44, mean age 26.16±6.27, 21M/23F) were collected for comparison but not used for normative model training. Normative certainty index showed high reliability (0.991 for aFCS, 0.990 for fFCS), and deviation rates in healthy Cam-CAN sample were close to expected 5% (supra-deviation: 2.75% aFCS, 2.91% fFCS; infra-deviation: 2.82% aFCS, 2.92% fFCS).
